title: DMARC
summary: DMARC, short for Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance, is a published policy that tells receiving mail systems what to do when a message claiming to be from your domain fails authentication. It is not itself an authentication mechanism. Instead it ties together two existing checks, SPF and DKIM, and requires that at least one of them pass and that the domain in the visible From header align with the domain those checks validated. The policy lives in a DNS TXT record at a reserved name under your domain and offers three main dispositions: monitor, quarantine, or reject. The same record asks receivers to send aggregate reports about the traffic they see and forensic reports about individual failures, which is how a domain owner discovers who is legitimately sending mail on their behalf. The mistake people usually make is jumping straight to a reject policy without first reading the reports, which silently blocks real business mail from forgotten senders such as ticketing systems or marketing platforms.

beginner.definition: DMARC stands for Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance. It is a public rule you publish about your own email domain. The rule tells other mail servers what to do with a failed message. Such a message pretends to come from you.
beginner.whyItMatters: Attackers often send fake invoices and password resets using a company name people trust. Those messages are hard for a person to spot. DMARC lets you tell the world to block or quarantine such mail. It also sends you reports about who is sending mail as your domain. Without it, anyone can forge your name and you will never know.
howItWorks: Your domain publishes a special DNS record that states your chosen policy.
The receiving server checks the sending server address and any DKIM signature on the message.
It then compares those checked domains with the domain shown in the visible From field.
If at least one check passes and the domains match, the message is trusted.
If both checks fail or the domains do not match, your published policy is applied.
You receive reports and use them to find every legitimate sender before you tighten the rule.
beginner.example: Imagine a company that issues staff badges. The badge reader checks the card and the photo, and it must agree with the name on the visitor list. If the card is fake, the guard follows a written rule: turn the visitor away, or hold them at reception. The rule also sends a weekly list of everyone who tried the door. The company then notices names it never issued badges to.
takeaways: DMARC is a policy plus reporting; it depends on SPF and DKIM doing the checking.
Start in monitoring mode, read the reports, then move slowly to a strict policy.
Alignment matters: the visible From domain must match the domain that passed a check.

objectives: Explain what DMARC is and why it is described as a policy rather than an authentication method.
Describe how SPF and DKIM checks are combined with domain alignment to reach a decision.
Interpret the meaning of the main policy dispositions a domain owner can publish.
Explain how aggregate reporting helps an organisation discover all legitimate senders.
Outline a safe rollout that avoids blocking genuine business email.
